title: Modules
summary: CommonJS vs ES Modules, module loading resolution, require cache, and module.exports.

explanation.overview: Node.js supports CommonJS (`require`/`module.exports`) and ES Modules (`import`/`export`).

sections.heading: CommonJS & require Cache
sections.content: CommonJS loads modules synchronously via `require()`. Resolved module exports are cached inside `require.cache`. Subsequent `require()` calls return cached singleton export.
bulletPoints: `module.exports`: Object exported by module.
`require.cache`: Caches resolved exports by absolute file path.
Singleton Behavior: Modules execute once upon initial require.

sections.heading: ES Modules (ESM) in Node.js
sections.content: Node enables ESM when `package.json` contains `"type": "module"` or files use `.mjs` extension.
bulletPoints: Package JSON: `"type": "module"` makes `.js` files ESM.
Extensions: Explicit file extensions (`./utils.js`) required in ESM imports.
Interoperability: ESM can import CommonJS, but CommonJS cannot use synchronous `require()` on ESM.

keyTakeaways: CommonJS uses `require`/`module.exports`; ESM uses `import`/`export`.
`require()` caches exports in `require.cache`.
Set `"type": "module"` in `package.json` to enable ES Modules natively.

codeExamples.title: CommonJS vs ESM Exports
codeExamples.description: Demonstrating CommonJS module.exports vs ESM default/named exports.

mcqs.question: What happens when a file is required twice `require('./db')` in CommonJS?
options: Node returns cached export from `require.cache` without re-executing file body
mcqs.explanation: CommonJS caches exported module object on first load; subsequent requires return cached instance.

mcqs.question: How do you enable native ES Modules (`import`/`export`) for all `.js` files in a Node.js project?
options: Add use esm at top of file
mcqs.explanation: Adding `"type": "module"` in `package.json` configures Node to treat `.js` files as ES Modules.

mcqs.question: What is `__dirname` variable inside CommonJS modules?
options: Absolute directory path of current module file
mcqs.explanation: `__dirname` holds absolute folder directory path of current CommonJS module file.

mcqs.question: Are `__dirname` and `__filename` available inside ES Modules (`.mjs`) by default?
options: No, ESM lacks __dirname (use import.meta.url and fileURLToPath)
mcqs.explanation: ES Modules do not define `__dirname` or `__filename`; construct them using `import.meta.url`.

mcqs.question: How do you export multiple items from a CommonJS module?
mcqs.explanation: CommonJS exports items by mutating `exports` object or assigning `module.exports`.

title: path
summary: Cross-platform path resolution: path.join, path.resolve, path.extname, and POSIX vs Windows differences.

explanation.overview: The `path` module provides utilities for handling and transforming file and directory paths across OS platforms (Windows backslashes `\` vs POSIX forward slashes `/`).

sections.heading: path.join vs path.resolve
sections.content: `path.join()` joins path segments using OS-specific delimiter. `path.resolve()` resolves segments into absolute path starting from current working directory.
bulletPoints: `path.join('a', 'b', 'c.js')`: Produces `'a/b/c.js'` (POSIX) or `'a\b\c.js'` (Windows).
`path.resolve('a', 'b')`: Resolves into full absolute path `/cwd/a/b`.
Normalization: Cleans `..` and `.` relative path segments automatically.

sections.heading: Path Parsing Utilities
sections.content: `path.extname()`, `path.basename()`, `path.dirname()`, and `path.parse()` extract path components.
bulletPoints: `path.extname('file.html')`: Returns extension `'.html'`.
`path.basename('/a/b/file.txt')`: Returns file name `'file.txt'`.
`path.parse(pathStr)`: Parses path into object `{ root, dir, base, ext, name }`.

keyTakeaways: Use `path.join()` for cross-platform relative path construction.
Use `path.resolve()` to create absolute path references.
Never hardcode `/` or `\` slash strings manually.

codeExamples.title: Path Utilities Overview
codeExamples.description: Using join, resolve, extname, and parse.

mcqs.question: What is key operational difference between `path.join()` and `path.resolve()`?
options: join returns Promise, resolve returns string
join concatenates path segments with OS delimiter; resolve always yields absolute path rooted from CWD
mcqs.explanation: `path.resolve()` resolves path segments into an absolute path prepending current working directory if unrooted.

mcqs.question: What does `path.extname('archive.tar.gz')` return?
mcqs.explanation: `path.extname()` returns substring from last dot `.` to end of string (`'.gz'`).

mcqs.question: Why should developers use `path.join(__dirname, 'file.json')` instead of `'/' + __dirname + '/file.json'`?
options: Handles OS-specific path separators automatically (Windows backslash `\` vs POSIX forward slash `/`)
mcqs.explanation: `path.join()` automatically uses host OS path separator (`\` vs `/`).

mcqs.question: What does `path.basename('/var/www/index.html', '.html')` return?
mcqs.explanation: Passing second extension argument to `path.basename` strips extension from returned name.

mcqs.question: Which method normalizes path string `'a/b/../c/./d'` by resolving `..` and `.` segments?
mcqs.explanation: `path.normalize()` resolves relative `..` and `.` segments into clean path string.

title: Express
summary: Express framework fundamentals, routing (app.get, app.post), req/res objects, and application structure.

explanation.overview: Express is minimal, fast, unopinionated web framework for Node.js providing robust routing and HTTP utility abstractions.

sections.heading: Express Application & Routing
sections.content: `const app = express()` instantiates application. Route handlers map HTTP methods and path patterns to handler callbacks `(req, res) => {}`.
bulletPoints: Routing: `app.get()`, `app.post()`, `app.put()`, `app.delete()`.
Route Params: `app.get('/users/:id')` accessed via `req.params.id`.
Query Strings: `req.query.search` for URL parameters (`?search=term`).

sections.heading: Response Helpers
sections.content: Express extends native response object with utility methods (`res.json()`, `res.status()`, `res.send()`, `res.redirect()`).
bulletPoints: `res.status(400).json({ error: 'Invalid' })`: Sets status and sends JSON.
`res.sendFile(path)`: Streams static file directly.

keyTakeaways: Express simplifies HTTP server routing and request/response manipulation.
Access route parameters via `req.params`, query params via `req.query`.
Use `res.status(code).json(body)` for API responses.

codeExamples.title: Express REST Router
codeExamples.description: Express app with route params, query params, and JSON response.

mcqs.question: How do you extract URL parameter `:id` in route `app.get('/items/:id', handler)`?
mcqs.explanation: Route path parameters matching `:paramName` reside inside `req.params` object.

mcqs.question: Which built-in Express middleware parses incoming JSON request bodies?
mcqs.explanation: `express.json()` middleware parses incoming JSON request payloads into `req.body`.

mcqs.question: What is proper way to return HTTP 404 JSON response in Express?
mcqs.explanation: `res.status(404).json({...})` sets status code and sends JSON body.

mcqs.question: How do you extract query parameters from URL `/search?term=phone&limit=10` in Express?
mcqs.explanation: URL query strings are automatically parsed into `req.query` object.

mcqs.question: What Express router method handles ALL HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) for a path?
mcqs.explanation: `app.all('/path', handler)` matches any HTTP request method target.

title: Middleware
summary: Express middleware pipeline, (req, res, next) signature, error-handling middleware, and execution chain.

explanation.overview: Middleware functions are functions with access to `req`, `res`, and `next` function in Express request-response cycle.

sections.heading: Middleware Pipeline & next()
sections.content: Middleware functions can execute code, modify `req`/`res` objects, end response cycle, or call `next()` to pass control to next middleware.
bulletPoints: Signature: `(req, res, next) => {}`.
Must Call `next()`: If middleware does not end response (`res.json()`), it MUST call `next()` to avoid hanging connection.
Global vs Route Middleware: `app.use(mw)` applies globally; `app.get('/path', mw, handler)` applies to specific route.

sections.heading: Error-Handling Middleware
sections.content: Error handling middleware requires FOUR parameters `(err, req, res, next)`. Passing an argument to `next(err)` skips normal middleware and jumps straight to error handlers.
bulletPoints: 4 Parameters: `(err, req, res, next)` signature identifies error handlers.
Trigger: Calling `next(err)` or throwing error in sync handler jumps to error middleware.

keyTakeaways: Middleware signature is `(req, res, next)`.
Always call `next()` unless ending request cycle.
Error-handling middleware requires 4 parameters `(err, req, res, next)`.

codeExamples.title: Custom Logger & Error Middleware
codeExamples.description: Request logger middleware and global error handling middleware.

mcqs.question: What is parameter signature of Express Error-Handling middleware?
mcqs.explanation: Express identifies error-handling middleware by its explicit 4-parameter signature `(err, req, res, next)`.

mcqs.question: What happens if a custom middleware does NOT call `next()` nor send a response (`res.send()`)?
options: Request hangs indefinitely until client connection times out
mcqs.explanation: Failing to invoke `next()` or terminate response cycle leaves request connection hanging.

mcqs.question: What happens when you pass an error argument `next(new Error('Auth failed'))` inside route handler?
options: Express skips all remaining normal middleware and routes to nearest 4-parameter error handler
mcqs.explanation: Passing any value to `next(err)` triggers Express error handling pipeline.

mcqs.question: In what order does Express execute registered middleware functions?
options: Sequential order in which they are declared using `app.use()`
mcqs.explanation: Middleware executes sequentially in exact order registered via `app.use()`.

mcqs.question: Which popular middleware adds CORS headers to Express responses?
mcqs.explanation: The `cors` package middleware enables Cross-Origin Resource Sharing in Express.

title: REST APIs
summary: RESTful API design, HTTP verb semantics, status code standards, resource routing, and JSON responses.

explanation.overview: REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style for designing networked APIs using standard HTTP verbs, resources, and status codes.

sections.heading: HTTP Verb Semantics
sections.content:
REST routes map resource nouns to HTTP verbs:
- `GET /api/v1/products`: List products.
- `POST /api/v1/products`: Create product.
- `PUT /api/v1/products/:id`: Replace product.
- `PATCH /api/v1/products/:id`: Partial update.
- `DELETE /api/v1/products/:id`: Delete product.
bulletPoints: Nouns over Verbs: `/api/users` instead of `/api/getUsers`.
Idempotency: GET, PUT, DELETE are idempotent; POST is non-idempotent.

sections.heading: Standard Status Codes
sections.content:
Return accurate HTTP status codes:
- `200 OK` / `201 Created` / `204 No Content`.
- `400 Bad Request` / `401 Unauthorized` / `403 Forbidden` / `404 Not Found`.
- `500 Internal Server Error`.
bulletPoints: 201 Created: Return upon successful POST resource creation.
401 vs 403: 401 = Missing/invalid auth token; 403 = Authenticated user lacks permission.

keyTakeaways: Use resource nouns in URL paths (`/api/orders`).
Use correct HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE).
Return accurate HTTP status codes (201 for POST creation, 401 vs 403).

codeExamples.title: Express REST API Endpoints
codeExamples.description: Standard REST endpoint handlers with correct status codes.

mcqs.question: Which HTTP status code should be returned after successfully creating a new resource via POST?
mcqs.explanation: `201 Created` indicates resource was created successfully.

mcqs.question: What is difference between HTTP `PUT` and `PATCH` methods in REST API design?
options: PUT is async, PATCH is sync
PUT replaces target resource completely; PATCH applies partial field updates
mcqs.explanation: `PUT` replaces resource entirely; `PATCH` updates specified fields partially.

mcqs.question: Which REST URL path naming convention follows best practices?
mcqs.explanation: REST APIs use plural resource nouns (`/api/v1/users`) rather than action verbs.

mcqs.question: What is distinction between `401 Unauthorized` and `403 Forbidden` status codes?
options: 401 means user is not authenticated; 403 means user is authenticated but lacks required permission scope
mcqs.explanation: 401 indicates unauthenticated user; 403 indicates authenticated user lacking permission.

mcqs.question: Which HTTP status code should be returned for successful `DELETE` request with no response body?
mcqs.explanation: `204 No Content` indicates request succeeded and response body is intentionally empty.

title: fs
summary: File system operations: reading, writing, appending, streams, watching files, and permissions.

explanation.overview: The `fs` (File System) module allows interacting with files and directories on host operating system.

sections.heading: File Reading & Writing
sections.content: Provides async callback, promise (`fs/promises`), and sync variants for file manipulations (`readFile`, `writeFile`, `appendFile`, `unlink`).
bulletPoints: Encoding: Specify `'utf-8'` to get string output instead of raw binary Buffer.
Write vs Append: `writeFile` overwrites existing content; `appendFile` adds content to end.
Unlink: `fs.unlink()` deletes file from disk.

sections.heading: Directory & File Watching
sections.content: `fs.mkdir()`, `fs.readdir()`, and `fs.watch()` manage directories and monitor file system changes.
bulletPoints: Recursive mkdir: `fs.mkdir(path, { recursive: true })` creates nested folders.
File Watcher: `fs.watch(filename, callback)` triggers events when files mutate.

keyTakeaways: Specify `'utf-8'` encoding when reading files as text.
Use `fs/promises` for async/await file operations.
Use streams (`createReadStream`) for large files to avoid memory bloat.

codeExamples.title: Async File Operations with fs/promises
codeExamples.description: Writing, appending, reading, and deleting files asynchronously.

mcqs.question: What is returned by `fs.readFile('./file.txt')` if encoding parameter is omitted?
mcqs.explanation: Without specifying text encoding (e.g. `'utf-8'`), `readFile` returns raw binary `Buffer`.

mcqs.question: Which method deletes a file from disk in Node.js?
mcqs.explanation: `fs.unlink()` (or `fs.rm()`) removes file from file system.

mcqs.question: How do you create nested parent and child directories `a/b/c` if they do not exist?
mcqs.explanation: Option `{ recursive: true }` instructs `mkdir` to create missing parent directories.

mcqs.question: Why is `fs.readFile()` dangerous for reading a 4GB video file into memory?
options: Attempts to load entire 4GB file into V8 RAM buffer at once, causing memory exhaustion crash
mcqs.explanation: `readFile` loads complete file content into heap memory at once, exceeding V8 buffer memory limits.

mcqs.question: Which method checks if a file exists asynchronously without throwing error?
mcqs.explanation: `fs.access()` checks file existence or user read/write permissions.

title: File uploads
summary: Handling multipart/form-data, Multer middleware, disk storage vs memory storage, and file validation.

explanation.overview: Handling file uploads in Node.js requires parsing `multipart/form-data` request payloads using middleware libraries like `multer` or `formidable`.

sections.heading: Multipart Parsing & Multer Storage
sections.content: Standard JSON body parsers cannot parse binary file streams. `multer` middleware parses multipart fields, offering `diskStorage` (saves directly to disk) or `memoryStorage` (buffers file in RAM).
bulletPoints: diskStorage: Saves file directly to uploads directory.
memoryStorage: Keeps file in `req.file.buffer` (ideal for direct S3 upload).
Single vs Multiple: `upload.single('avatar')` vs `upload.array('photos', 5)`.

sections.heading: File Security & Validation
sections.content: Never trust client-provided file extension or `file.mimetype`. Validate magic bytes (file signature), limit file size, and sanitize output file names.
bulletPoints: File Size Limits: `limits: { fileSize: 5 * 1024 * 1024 }` (5MB).
Magic Bytes: Check actual binary header bytes to prevent malware spoofing.
Random Filenames: Generate UUID filenames to prevent path traversal attacks.

keyTakeaways: Use `multer` to handle `multipart/form-data` file uploads.
Use `memoryStorage` for cloud S3 uploads; `diskStorage` for local file saving.
Validate file size limits and binary file headers (magic bytes) for security.

codeExamples.title: Express Multer File Upload Route
codeExamples.description: Configuring Multer diskStorage with size limits and file filter.

mcqs.question: What HTTP `Content-Type` header format is required for submitting file uploads from forms?
mcqs.explanation: File uploads require `multipart/form-data` encoding format.

mcqs.question: Which Multer storage engine keeps uploaded file contents in `req.file.buffer` RAM for streaming to AWS S3?
mcqs.explanation: `multer.memoryStorage()` retains uploaded binary file in `req.file.buffer` RAM.

mcqs.question: Why should uploaded files be saved with randomly generated UUIDs instead of original `file.originalname`?
options: Prevents path traversal attacks (`../../etc/passwd`) and file overwrite collisions
mcqs.explanation: Original filenames can contain malicious path traversal dots (`../`) or duplicate name collisions.

mcqs.question: How do you enforce a maximum file size limit (e.g. 5MB) in Multer?
mcqs.explanation: Multer accepts `limits: { fileSize: bytes }` configuration option.

mcqs.question: Why is checking file extension `.png` insufficient for security validation?
options: Attackers can rename malicious `.php` or `.exe` files to `.png`; magic binary header bytes must be verified
Extensions do not exist on Linux
mcqs.explanation: File extensions are easily spoofed; server must inspect actual magic binary header bytes.

title: Events
summary: EventEmitter class, on, once, emit, removeListener, handling error events.

explanation.overview: The `events` module provides `EventEmitter` class, backbone of event-driven architecture in Node.js core modules (http, net, streams).

sections.heading: EventEmitter Fundamentals
sections.content: Objects extend `EventEmitter` to emit named events that trigger registered listener functions.
bulletPoints: `on(event, listener)`: Registers persistent listener callback.
`once(event, listener)`: Registers one-time listener that automatically unregisters after first trigger.
`emit(event, ...args)`: Synchronously calls all registered listeners with arguments.

sections.heading: Special 'error' Event & Listener Leaks
sections.content: If an `EventEmitter` emits `'error'` event without at least ONE listener attached, Node.js throws uncaught exception and crashes process.
bulletPoints: Error Event Rule: Always attach `.on('error', handler)` listener.
Max Listeners Warning: Warning emitted if > 10 listeners are attached (configurable via `setMaxListeners()`).

keyTakeaways: `EventEmitter` powers event-driven architecture in Node.
Always attach listener for `'error'` events to prevent process crashes.
Use `.once()` for one-time event triggers.

codeExamples.title: Custom EventEmitter Class
codeExamples.description: Extending EventEmitter and emitting custom events.

mcqs.question: What happens if an `EventEmitter` instance emits an `'error'` event when NO listener is registered for `'error'`?
options: Node.js prints stacktrace and crashes application process
mcqs.explanation: Unhandled `'error'` events in EventEmitter throw uncaught exception, crashing Node process.

mcqs.question: What is difference between `.on()` and `.once()` methods in EventEmitter?
options: on is async, once is sync
once automatically removes listener callback after it triggers for the first time
mcqs.explanation: `.once()` unregisters listener automatically after single execution.

mcqs.question: Are event listeners invoked synchronously or asynchronously by default when `emitter.emit('event')` is called?
mcqs.explanation: `EventEmitter.emit()` calls registered listener functions synchronously in order.

mcqs.question: What is default maximum number of listeners allowed on single event before EventEmitter prints memory leak warning?
mcqs.explanation: Default max listeners limit is 10 (changeable via `emitter.setMaxListeners(n)`).

mcqs.question: How do you unregister a specific listener function `fn` from event `'userLogin'`?
mcqs.explanation: `removeListener()` or alias `off()` unregisters specific callback function reference.

title: Buffer
summary: Binary data storage, V8 heap allocation, Buffer.from, Buffer.alloc, encodings (utf-8, base64, hex).

explanation.overview: `Buffer` objects represent fixed-length sequences of raw binary bytes allocated outside V8 heap in memory.

sections.heading: Buffer Allocation: alloc vs allocUnsafe
sections.content: `Buffer.alloc(size)` allocates memory zero-filled for security. `Buffer.allocUnsafe(size)` allocates raw memory quickly without zero-filling (may contain sensitive old memory data).
bulletPoints: `Buffer.alloc(size)`: Safe zero-filled memory allocation.
`Buffer.allocUnsafe(size)`: Fast uninitialized allocation; must overwrite immediately.
`Buffer.from(str, encoding)`: Creates Buffer from string/array.

sections.heading: Encodings & Conversion
sections.content: Buffers support encodings: `'utf-8'`, `'base64'`, `'hex'`, `'latin1'`. Converting buffers to strings uses `buf.toString(encoding)`.
bulletPoints: Base64: `buf.toString('base64')` for file encoding.
Hex: `buf.toString('hex')` for hash digests.

keyTakeaways: Buffers handle raw binary data allocated outside V8 heap.
Use `Buffer.alloc()` for safe zero-filled memory allocation.
Use `buf.toString('base64')` or `buf.toString('hex')` to convert binary buffers.

codeExamples.title: Buffer Creation & Encoding Conversion
codeExamples.description: Creating buffers from string, hex, and converting to base64.

mcqs.question: Where is memory allocated for Node.js `Buffer` objects?
options: Outside V8 heap in raw un-managed C++ memory pool
mcqs.explanation: Buffers allocate memory outside V8 heap using `ArrayBuffer` backing store.

mcqs.question: Why is `Buffer.allocUnsafe(100)` potentially security-sensitive if output is sent directly to client?
options: Un-initialized allocated memory bytes may contain un-cleared sensitive residual memory data
mcqs.explanation: `allocUnsafe` skips zero-filling memory; old sensitive memory fragments might be exposed.

mcqs.question: How do you convert a string `'Hello'` to a binary Buffer object?
mcqs.explanation: Static method `Buffer.from(str, encoding)` creates a Buffer from string input.

mcqs.question: Which buffer method converts binary data to Base64 encoded string?
mcqs.explanation: `buf.toString('base64')` encodes buffer binary bytes into Base64 ASCII string.

mcqs.question: Is Buffer size fixed after creation `const buf = Buffer.alloc(10)`?
options: Yes, Buffer instances have immutable fixed memory length once allocated
mcqs.explanation: Node Buffers have fixed memory byte lengths established upon allocation.

title: HTTP
summary: Core http module, createServer, req/res streams, status codes, and header management.

explanation.overview: The built-in `http` module allows building web servers and HTTP clients without external dependencies.

sections.heading: http.createServer & Stream Handling
sections.content: `http.createServer((req, res) => {})` initializes HTTP server. `req` is Readable stream of incoming request data; `res` is Writable stream for sending response.
bulletPoints: `req` (IncomingMessage): Readable stream (headers, method, url, body chunks).
`res` (ServerResponse): Writable stream (`writeHead`, `setHeader`, `write`, `end`).
Port Listening: `server.listen(port, callback)`.

sections.heading: Request Body Parsing
sections.content: Incoming POST request bodies stream in chunks over `req.on('data')` events. Assemble buffer chunks before parsing JSON.
bulletPoints: Data Event: `req.on('data', chunk => chunks.push(chunk))`.
End Event: `req.on('end', () => JSON.parse(Buffer.concat(chunks)))`.

keyTakeaways: `http.createServer` handles request and response streams.
`req` is a Readable stream; `res` is a Writable stream.
Always call `res.end()` to complete HTTP response.

codeExamples.title: Native Node.js HTTP Server
codeExamples.description: Creating HTTP server with status code, headers, and JSON body.

mcqs.question: What type of stream is `req` object inside `http.createServer((req, res) => {})`?
mcqs.explanation: Incoming request `req` is a `Readable` stream emitting incoming data chunks.

mcqs.question: What happens if you forget to invoke `res.end()` in a Node.js HTTP request handler?
options: Client connection hangs waiting for server response until client times out
mcqs.explanation: Without `res.end()`, HTTP response stream remains open, hanging client connection.

mcqs.question: Which method sets HTTP status code and response headers simultaneously on response stream?
mcqs.explanation: `res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'text/html' })` writes status code and headers in single call.

mcqs.question: How do you collect incoming POST body data from raw `req` readable stream?
options: Listen to `req.on('data', chunk => ...)` and `req.on('end', ...)` stream events
mcqs.explanation: Raw HTTP request data arrives in chunks via `data` events, assembled on `end` event.

mcqs.question: Which core module makes outgoing HTTP requests to external APIs natively in Node?
mcqs.explanation: Native `http` and `https` modules provide `http.request()` and `https.get()` methods.

title: Async I/O
summary: Non-blocking asynchronous input/output, callback conventions, error-first callbacks, promise-based APIs.

explanation.overview: Non-blocking Asynchronous I/O is Node core philosophy. Disk files and network sockets operate asynchronously without blocking main thread execution.

sections.heading: Error-First Callback Pattern
sections.content: Traditional Node asynchronous functions take a callback whose first argument is error `(err, result) => {}`.
bulletPoints: First Argument `err`: Null/undefined on success, Error object on failure.
Callback Hell: Deeply nested callbacks solved by Promises/async-await.

sections.heading: Promises & fs/promises
sections.content: Modern Node modules expose promise-based variants (`require('fs/promises')`), allowing clean `async/await` syntax.
bulletPoints: fs/promises: Promise wrappers for file operations.
util.promisify(): Converts legacy error-first callback functions into Promise functions.

keyTakeaways: Node I/O operations are non-blocking and asynchronous by default.
Follow error-first callback convention `(err, data)` for legacy callbacks.
Use `fs/promises` and `async/await` for modern readable async code.

codeExamples.title: fs/promises vs promisify
codeExamples.description: Using fs/promises and util.promisify for non-blocking I/O.

mcqs.question: What is Node.js standard convention for callback parameter order?
mcqs.explanation: Node.js standard convention mandates Error as first argument `(err, data)`.

mcqs.question: Which core utility function converts legacy error-first callback functions to return Promises?
mcqs.explanation: `util.promisify(fn)` converts standard error-first callback functions into Promise-returning functions.

mcqs.question: What is drawback of using synchronous file methods like `fs.readFileSync()` in a production web server?
options: Blocks main thread completely while reading file from disk, stalling all concurrent HTTP requests
mcqs.explanation: Synchronous file methods block single main thread, stalling all active server connections.

mcqs.question: Which module import provides native Promise-based file system methods in modern Node.js?
mcqs.explanation: `require('fs/promises')` or `import fs from 'node:fs/promises'` exports Promise-based file system methods.

mcqs.question: How does Node async I/O handle underlying OS file operations without blocking JS thread?
options: Delegating task to libuv C++ thread pool and pushing callback to event loop upon completion
mcqs.explanation: libuv offloads OS file I/O to worker thread pool, notifying JS event loop upon completion.

title: Node architecture
summary: Single-threaded event loop, V8 engine, libuv thread pool, and non-blocking asynchronous I/O model.

explanation.overview: Node.js is an open-source, cross-platform JavaScript runtime environment built on Chrome V8 engine. Node uses single-threaded event loop architecture powered by libuv for non-blocking I/O.

sections.heading: Single Threaded Event Loop & libuv
sections.content: JavaScript code executes on a single main thread. Underlying I/O operations (file system, network DNS, compression) are offloaded to C++ libuv thread pool (default 4 worker threads).
bulletPoints: Main Thread: Executes JS call stack synchronous code.
libuv C++ Pool: Handles disk I/O, DNS lookup, and cryptographic work.
Non-blocking: Asynchronous operations register callbacks and yield main thread.

sections.heading: Node Core Stack Components
sections.content: V8 compiles JS to machine code; libuv provides event loop and OS abstraction; C++ bindings bridge JS calls to OS native APIs.
bulletPoints: V8 Engine: Executes JS code.
libuv: Manages event loop and asynchronous thread pool.
Node.js Bindings: Expose OS level capabilities (fs, net, crypto) to JS.

keyTakeaways: Node.js is single-threaded for JS execution, multi-threaded under the hood via libuv.
libuv manages asynchronous I/O tasks and default 4-thread pool.
Never block the main thread with synchronous CPU operations.

codeExamples.title: Non-blocking Async I/O
codeExamples.description: Reading file asynchronously without blocking main thread.

mcqs.question: What is primary role of `libuv` in Node.js architecture?
options: Managing Event Loop and underlying OS asynchronous I/O thread pool
mcqs.explanation: `libuv` is C library providing Event Loop and thread pool for async OS I/O tasks.

mcqs.question: How many default worker threads exist in libuv thread pool?
mcqs.explanation: Default libuv thread pool size is 4 (configurable via `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE`).

mcqs.question: What executes JavaScript code inside Node.js runtime?
mcqs.explanation: Node.js runs Google Chrome V8 engine to compile and execute JS code.

mcqs.question: Why is Node.js well suited for I/O-intensive real-time applications?
options: Non-blocking event loop handles thousands of concurrent socket connections efficiently without thread overhead
mcqs.explanation: Non-blocking event-driven architecture handles massive concurrent I/O requests with low memory footprint.

mcqs.question: What happens if heavy synchronous CPU loop executes on Node main thread?
options: Main thread blocks, stalling all incoming network requests and event callbacks
mcqs.explanation: Synchronous CPU loops block single main thread, freezing server request processing.

title: Streams
summary: Processing large data chunk by chunk, Readable, Writable, Duplex, Transform streams, and pipe().

explanation.overview: Streams handle reading or writing data chunk-by-chunk asynchronously without loading entire datasets into memory.

sections.heading: 4 Fundamental Stream Types
sections.content:
1. **Readable**: Data source stream (`fs.createReadStream`, `req`).
2. **Writable**: Data sink destination stream (`fs.createWriteStream`, `res`).
3. **Duplex**: Readable and Writable stream (TCP sockets).
4. **Transform**: Duplex stream that modifies data while reading/writing (`zlib.createGzip`).
bulletPoints: Readable: Emits `data`, `end`, `error` events.
Writable: Implements `write()`, `end()`, `finish` event.
Transform: Modifies data (encryption, compression).

sections.heading: Piping & pipeline Utility
sections.content: `readable.pipe(writable)` connects readable stream to writable stream. Use `stream.pipeline` for proper error propagation and cleanup.
bulletPoints: pipe(): `readStream.pipe(writeStream)`.
pipeline(): `pipeline(readStream, transformStream, writeStream, callback)` handles error cleanup.

keyTakeaways: Streams process data sequentially in memory-efficient chunks.
4 Stream Types: Readable, Writable, Duplex, Transform.
Use `pipeline()` instead of `.pipe()` to handle error destruction automatically.

codeExamples.title: Gzip File Compression Pipeline Stream
codeExamples.description: Streaming large file through Gzip transform into write stream.

mcqs.question: What is main advantage of using Streams to handle 10GB file uploads?
options: Processes file chunk by chunk in memory (~64KB buffer), keeping RAM usage flat
mcqs.explanation: Streams process data in small chunks, using constant low RAM regardless of file size.

mcqs.question: Which stream type is `zlib.createGzip()` compression stream?
mcqs.explanation: Transform streams are Duplex streams that transform data while streaming.

mcqs.question: Why is `stream.pipeline()` preferred over standard `.pipe()` chaining?
options: pipeline automatically cleans up and destroys streams when errors occur
mcqs.explanation: `pipeline()` forwards errors and properly closes/destroys all chained streams upon failure.

mcqs.question: Which event is emitted by a Readable stream when all data chunks have been read?
mcqs.explanation: Readable streams emit `end` event when no more data chunks remain.

mcqs.question: Which event is emitted by a Writable stream when all queued data has been written to underlying target?
mcqs.explanation: Writable streams emit `finish` event after `stream.end()` completes writing.

title: Backpressure
summary: Stream rate management, readable buffer vs writable buffer, highWaterMark, drain event.

explanation.overview: Backpressure occurs in stream data processing when data is produced faster by Readable stream than can be consumed by Writable destination stream.

sections.heading: highWaterMark & Buffer Saturation
sections.content: Streams store chunks in internal buffer bounded by `highWaterMark` (default 16KB for normal streams, 64KB for fs). When Writable buffer exceeds `highWaterMark`, `writable.write()` returns `false`.
bulletPoints: write() returns false: Indicates destination buffer is full.
Pause Reading: Producer must pause sending data chunks when write returns false.

sections.heading: Handling Backpressure with drain Event
sections.content: When Writable destination finishes processing queued buffer, it emits `drain` event. Producer resumes reading data upon receiving `drain` event.
bulletPoints: `drain` Event: Signals Writable stream is ready for more data.
`pipe()` & `pipeline()`: Automatically manage backpressure and `drain` events.

keyTakeaways: Backpressure prevents fast producers from overwhelming slow consumers in RAM.
When `writable.write()` returns `false`, pause the readable stream.
Resume reading when writable stream emits `drain` event.

codeExamples.title: Manual Backpressure Management
codeExamples.description: Pausing read stream on false write and resuming on drain event.

mcqs.question: What is 'Backpressure' in Node.js streams?
options: Condition where Readable stream produces data faster than Writable stream can consume, causing buffer growth in RAM
mcqs.explanation: Backpressure arises when data production outpaces consumption rate, risking memory exhaustion.

mcqs.question: What does `writable.write(chunk)` return when internal buffer exceeds `highWaterMark` limit?
mcqs.explanation: `write()` returns `false` to signal producer to pause pushing data chunks.

mcqs.question: Which event emitted by Writable stream signals producer that buffer has emptied and reading can resume?
mcqs.explanation: `drain` event notifies producer that Writable stream buffer cleared and can accept more data.

mcqs.question: What is default `highWaterMark` buffer size for standard non-file Streams in Node.js?
mcqs.explanation: Default `highWaterMark` for standard streams is 16KB (16384 bytes).

mcqs.question: Do `.pipe()` and `stream.pipeline()` handle backpressure automatically?
options: Yes, they automatically pause and resume streams based on `highWaterMark` and `drain` events
mcqs.explanation: Built-in `.pipe()` and `pipeline()` manage backpressure and `drain` events under the hood.

title: Error handling
summary: Operational vs Programmer errors, uncaughtException, unhandledRejection, and graceful shutdown.

explanation.overview: Proper error handling in Node.js distinguishes operational errors from programmer bugs and ensures graceful server shutdown during critical failures.

sections.heading: Operational vs Programmer Errors
sections.content: **Operational Errors** represent runtime problems (network timeouts, invalid user inputs, DB connection lost). **Programmer Errors** are bugs (null pointer dereferences, syntax errors, bad function arguments).
bulletPoints: Operational: Expected runtime failures; handle gracefully with error status codes.
Programmer: Code bugs; log stacktrace and restart process using process manager (PM2/K8s).

sections.heading: Uncaught Exceptions & Graceful Shutdown
sections.content: Listen to `uncaughtException` and `unhandledRejection` process events. When fatal error occurs, stop receiving new HTTP requests, close database pools, and exit process (`process.exit(1)`).
bulletPoints: `process.on('uncaughtException')`: Catches unhandled synchronous errors.
`process.on('unhandledRejection')`: Catches unhandled promise rejections.
Graceful Exit: `server.close(() => process.exit(1))`.

keyTakeaways: Distinguish operational runtime errors from programmer bugs.
Do NOT leave process running in corrupted state after `uncaughtException`.
Perform graceful shutdown (close server & DB connections) before `process.exit(1)`.

codeExamples.title: Graceful Server Shutdown Pattern
codeExamples.description: Handling uncaughtException and closing server gracefully.

mcqs.question: What is an example of an Operational Error in a Node.js web server?
options: Database query timeout or invalid user login credentials
mcqs.explanation: Operational errors are expected runtime failure conditions like database timeouts or bad input.

mcqs.question: Why is it unsafe to keep a Node.js process running after an `uncaughtException` event?
options: Application state is un-deterministic and corrupted; subsequent requests may leak data or deadlock
mcqs.explanation: Uncaught exceptions leave application state unpredictable; process should be restarted.

mcqs.question: Which process event catches unhandled Promise rejections in Node.js?
mcqs.explanation: `unhandledRejection` process event catches rejected promises lacking `.catch()`.

mcqs.question: What process exit code `process.exit(code)` indicates failure exit?
mcqs.explanation: Exit code `0` indicates success exit; non-zero codes (like `1`) indicate failure exit.

mcqs.question: What signal does container orchestrator (Kubernetes / Docker) send to request graceful application shutdown?
mcqs.explanation: `SIGTERM` signal notifies application to finish active requests and shut down gracefully.

title: Event loop
summary: Phases of Node event loop: Timers, Pending Callbacks, Idle/Prepare, Poll, Check, Close callbacks.

explanation.overview: The Node.js Event Loop handles asynchronous I/O callbacks across 6 distinct phases managed by libuv.

sections.heading: 6 Phases of Node.js Event Loop
sections.content:
1. **Timers**: Executes callbacks scheduled by `setTimeout()` and `setInterval()`.
2. **Pending Callbacks**: Executes I/O callbacks deferred to next loop iteration.
3. **Idle, Prepare**: Used internally by Node.
4. **Poll**: Retrieves new I/O events; executes I/O callbacks.
5. **Check**: Executes `setImmediate()` callbacks.
6. **Close Callbacks**: Executes close event handlers (`socket.on('close')`).
bulletPoints: Timers: Checks expired timer callbacks.
Poll: Blocks briefly waiting for incoming I/O events.
Check: Dedicated phase for `setImmediate()` callbacks.

sections.heading: process.nextTick vs setImmediate
sections.content: `process.nextTick()` is NOT part of libuv event loop phases; it runs immediately after current operation completes before transitioning to ANY phase. `setImmediate()` runs during Check phase.
bulletPoints: process.nextTick: Runs before next event loop phase transition.
setImmediate: Runs in Check phase after Poll phase.

keyTakeaways: Node event loop has 6 distinct libuv phases.
`setImmediate()` runs in the Check phase.
`process.nextTick()` executes before transitioning to next event loop phase.

codeExamples.title: process.nextTick vs setImmediate Order
codeExamples.description: Comparing execution order of nextTick, setImmediate, and setTimeout.

mcqs.question: In which phase of Node.js Event Loop do `setImmediate()` callbacks execute?
mcqs.explanation: `setImmediate()` callbacks are executed specifically during Check phase.

mcqs.question: When does `process.nextTick()` callback execute relative to Event Loop phases?
options: Immediately after current JavaScript call stack completes before transitioning to next Event Loop phase
mcqs.explanation: `process.nextTick()` drains immediately prior to shifting into any event loop phase.

mcqs.question: Which phase retrieves new I/O events and executes pending I/O callbacks?
mcqs.explanation: Poll phase polls for new I/O events and executes incoming I/O callbacks.

mcqs.question: What happens if `process.nextTick()` recursively calls `process.nextTick()` endlessly?
options: Starves Event Loop completely, preventing phase transitions and I/O callbacks
mcqs.explanation: Recursive `nextTick` calls starve the event loop by preventing it from reaching Poll phase.

mcqs.question: In which phase do `socket.on('close', fn)` callbacks execute?
mcqs.explanation: Close callbacks (`socket.on('close')`) are handled in Close Callbacks phase.

title: V8
summary: Google V8 engine architecture, JIT compilation (Ignition & TurboFan), memory heaps, and optimization flags.

explanation.overview: V8 is Google open-source high-performance C++ JavaScript engine that compiles JS directly to native machine code using Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation.

sections.heading: Ignition Interpreter & TurboFan Compiler
sections.content: V8 uses **Ignition** interpreter to generate bytecode from AST quickly. Hot functions identified by profiler are passed to **TurboFan** optimizing compiler to generate optimized machine code.
bulletPoints: Ignition: Generates and executes bytecode quickly.
TurboFan: Optimizes hot code paths using type feedback.
Deoptimization: Bailout to bytecode when hidden class shapes change dynamically.

sections.heading: Hidden Classes & Inline Caching
sections.content: V8 creates internal **Hidden Classes** (Shapes) for JS objects. Accessing object properties in consistent key order allows V8 to utilize Inline Caching for fast property lookups.
bulletPoints: Monomorphic Callsites: Identical object hidden class shapes yield maximum optimization.
Optimization Tip: Always initialize object properties in identical order inside constructors.

keyTakeaways: V8 compiles JS to machine code via JIT (Ignition + TurboFan).
Consistent object property initialization enables Hidden Class optimizations.
Avoid dynamic property deletion (`delete obj.prop`) to prevent deoptimization.

codeExamples.title: V8 Hidden Class Optimization Pattern
codeExamples.description: Consistent property assignment vs dynamic deletion.

mcqs.question: What is primary role of V8 TurboFan compiler?
options: JIT compile hot bytecode functions into highly optimized native machine code
mcqs.explanation: TurboFan optimizes hot bytecode paths compiled from Ignition into native machine code.

mcqs.question: What is a V8 'Hidden Class' (Shape)?
options: Internal layout structure created by V8 to optimize object property access offsets in memory
mcqs.explanation: V8 generates hidden classes to map object property offsets in memory for fast lookup.

mcqs.question: Why does calling `delete obj.prop` harm V8 execution performance?
options: Mutates object hidden class shape, forcing V8 into slow dictionary mode (deoptimization)
mcqs.explanation: `delete` changes object shape graph dynamically, forcing V8 to abandon fast inline caching.

mcqs.question: Which V8 component initially parses AST into bytecode?
mcqs.explanation: Ignition is V8's fast bytecode interpreter.

mcqs.question: Which command line flag increases V8 heap memory limit in Node.js (e.g. to 4GB)?
mcqs.explanation: `--max-old-space-size=4096` configures V8 old space memory limit in megabytes.
